questions.q: A service caches each request's cart object in a module-level Map and never deletes entries. Why is this a memory leak?
questions.explain: A Map holds its keys and values strongly. Anything reachable from a long-lived map stays in memory until you delete it.
options: Because Map copies every object it stores
The map refers to every cart, so none of them can be freed after its request ends, and the map grows with every request
Because maps are slower than objects
It is not a leak: the garbage collector removes old map entries automatically

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Maps and sets use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and 0 equals -0. So the set holds just NaN and 0.
questions.code:
const prices = new Map([[NaN, "unknown"], [0, "free"]]);
console.log(prices.get(NaN), prices.get(-0), new Set([NaN, NaN, 0, -0]).size);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Array keys are compared by identity. The literal in get creates a new array, so it never matches. Only the stored key object finds its entry.

questions.q: What is a safe way to key delivery fees by product and city, where city names are free text typed by staff?
questions.explain: Arrays and objects are keyed by identity. Plain concatenation can merge different pairs ("ab"+"c" and "a"+"bc"). Nested maps and JSON-encoded pairs keep the parts distinct.
options: Nested maps (product → city → fee), or a key built with JSON.stringify([sku, city])

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both concatenations produce "a|b|". JSON.stringify quotes each part, so the two pairs stay different.
questions.code:
const keyOf = (a, b) => `${a}|${b}`;
console.log(keyOf("a|b", "") === keyOf("a", "b|"), JSON.stringify(["a|b", ""]) === JSON.stringify(["a", "b|"]));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Setting an existing key keeps its position. Deleting and adding it again moves it to the end.

questions.q: In an LRU cache built on a Map, why is map.keys().next().value the key to evict?
questions.explain: Insertion order plus "move to the end on use" gives a recency order for free, and reading the first key is O(1).
options: Every read and write deletes and re-adds its key, moving it to the end, so the first key in insertion order is the least recently used
Because the first key is always the smallest

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An entry deleted before the loop reaches it is skipped, and an entry added during the loop is visited later in the same loop.

questions.q: A loop over a Set must add new items to that same set as it goes. How do you make sure it only visits the items that were there at the start?
questions.explain: Items added during iteration are visited, so a loop that keeps adding can run forever. A copied array fixes the list of items to visit.
options: Iterate over a snapshot, for (const x of [...set]), and add to the real set
Nothing is needed; new items are never visited

questions.q: An LRU cache holds at most 2 keys; get moves a key to the most recent position. What does this print?
questions.explain: After RICE, OIL, RICE the order is OIL, RICE. SALT makes three keys, so the oldest, OIL, is evicted.

questions.q: A cache's get decides "hit or miss" with if (value !== undefined). A product's cached price can be 0 and some cached lookups are legitimately undefined. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: !== undefined handles 0 correctly but not cached undefined. A truthiness check (if (value)) would also get 0 wrong. has answers the real question.
options: Cached undefined values are treated as misses and recomputed every time; use has(key) to decide instead
Prices of 0 are treated as misses
The cache evicts the wrong entry

questions.q: An LRU cache has room for 3 products, and customers keep cycling through the same 4 products in order. What happens?
questions.explain: LRU works when the working set fits in the cache. Size it for the keys in active use, and measure the hit rate.
options: Almost every request misses, because each new product evicts the one that will be needed next
Every request hits after the first round

questions.q: What does a time-to-live (TTL) on cache entries bound?
questions.explain: A size limit bounds memory; a TTL bounds staleness. Deleting an entry when its data changes makes it fresh immediately.
options: The memory used by the cache
How stale a cached value can be: after the TTL, the next read goes back to the source

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The set methods accept any set-like object: one with size, has and keys. A Map qualifies, using its keys. BEANS is in the map but not in the cart, so it is not in the intersection.
options: TypeError: stock is not a Set

questions.q: Why does new Set(["A"]).union(["B"]) throw a TypeError?
questions.explain: Wrap the array first: set.union(new Set(array)). The error message, "The .size property is NaN", comes from reading undefined as a size.
options: An array is not set-like: it has no size property (and no has), so the method rejects it
Because union is not supported in Node.js

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A set compares objects by identity, so all three stay. The map keyed by id lets the later event overwrite the value while ORD-1 keeps its first position.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object.groupBy turns keys into strings; Map.groupBy keeps the real boolean keys. Groups appear in the order their key was first seen.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify sees maps and sets as objects with no own enumerable properties and prints {}, without an error. Convert them explicitly.

questions.q: How do you copy a Map of sets so that changing the copy's inner sets does not change the original?
questions.explain: new Map(original) copies only one level: the inner sets are shared. Spread produces an empty object, and JSON loses the map entirely. structuredClone deep-copies maps and sets.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Weak keys must be able to die. Objects and ordinary symbols can; a string or a registered symbol from Symbol.for can always be recreated, so it is refused.

questions.q: Why does a WeakMap have no size, no keys() and no iteration?
questions.explain: Hiding the contents is what lets the engine drop entries freely. You can only ask about a key you already hold.
options: Entries can disappear whenever the garbage collector runs; exposing the contents would make program behaviour depend on when collection happens
Because it stores only one entry

questions.q: Which cache is a good fit for a WeakMap?
questions.explain: WeakMaps need object keys, and they shine when the key object defines how long the data is useful. Primitive keys need a Map with a size limit and TTL.
options: Product prices keyed by SKU string
A computed total keyed by a cart object, needed only while that cart is in use
Exchange rates keyed by currency code
User sessions keyed by session id

questions.q: A cart total is cached in a WeakMap keyed by the cart object. Code then pushes a new line into the same cart. What does the cache return next time?
questions.explain: Identity-keyed caches cannot see changes inside the key. Immutable values (a new object for every change) make every change a new key.
options: The new total, because the cache notices the change
The old total, because the key is still the same object; make carts immutable or clear the entry when the cart changes
Nothing, because changing an object removes it from WeakMaps

questions.q: Several middleware functions need to attach data to a frozen request object provided by a library. What does the lesson recommend?
questions.explain: WeakMaps attach data to objects you cannot or should not modify, keep it private to the code holding the map, and let it disappear with the request.
options: Unfreeze the request and add properties
A global array of [request, data] pairs
One WeakMap per kind of data, keyed by the request object
Copy the request with spread and add properties to the copy

questions.q: This toPlain marks objects on the current path in a WeakSet. What does it print for a shared, non-circular address?
questions.explain: The address is removed from seen after the billing branch finishes, so the shipping branch visits it again. Only objects that appear on their own path are cycles.
options: TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON

questions.q: What does a FinalizationRegistry callback guarantee?
questions.explain: Collection timing is up to the engine. Close files, release locks and save data explicitly, with try...finally.
options: It runs immediately after the object becomes unreachable
It runs before the process exits
Almost nothing: it may run some time after collection, or never, so it must not be used for program logic
It runs exactly once per registered object, at a predictable time

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: report is still referenced by a variable, so it cannot have been collected; deref returns the same object. After the last strong reference is gone it may return undefined.

questions.q: Which should be a plain object rather than a Map?
questions.explain: A record with a fixed set of known field names is an object. Collections of entries keyed by data are dictionaries, and Map fits them better.
options: A single order with fields id, status and totalKobo

questions.q: A shop runs four Node.js processes behind a load balancer, each with an in-memory price cache. An admin changes a price and the handling process deletes its cache entry. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Either accept staleness up to the TTL, broadcast invalidations, or use a shared cache when instances must agree.
options: The deleted entry comes back automatically
The other three processes still serve the old price until their own entries expire; in-memory caches are per process

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Updating an existing key keeps its position, so the map is in order of first appearance: OIL, RICE, SALT.

questions.q: Which job suits a WeakSet?
questions.explain: A WeakSet holds objects weakly and can only answer "is this object marked?". It cannot count, hold strings or be listed.
options: Counting how many times each product was viewed
Storing the ids of customers who opted out of email
Marking request objects that have already been logged, so middleware does not log them twice
Listing all active sessions for an admin page

questions.q: A dictionary is keyed by product codes typed by staff, and one code is "constructor". Why is a Map safer than a plain object here?
questions.explain: Keys from data belong in a Map (or an Object.create(null) object). Hash maps covered the full list of object traps.
options: A plain object already "has" inherited keys such as constructor and __proto__, so lookups and writes can hit the prototype; a Map has no inherited keys
Plain objects cannot have more than 1,000 keys

questions.q: Two requests ask for the same uncached, slow catalogue entry at the same moment, and both go to the database. What change makes the second request wait for the first load instead?
questions.explain: Storing the in-flight promise collapses concurrent loads into one. Remove it from the cache if the load fails, or the failure is cached too.
options: Caching the promise of the value as soon as the load starts, so the second request finds and awaits it

questions.q: Turning a cache off makes one test fail with a different total. What does that tell you?
questions.explain: A correct cache is invisible except for speed. Comparing results with the cache on and off is a good test.
options: The test is wrong: caches are supposed to change results
The cache has a bug, such as stale data or a key that is not unique enough, because a cache should only change speed, never results
The TTL is too long, which is fine

questions.q: Finish the LruCache class: get(key) returns the value and marks the key as most recently used (or returns undefined), and set(key, value) stores it as most recent and evicts the least recently used key when there are more than max entries.
questions.explain: Delete-and-set moves a key to the end, so the first key is always the least recently used. Reading RICE saved it; OIL was evicted.

questions.q: Write memoizeByObject(fn) using a WeakMap, so fn runs at most once per object, including when it returns undefined. The program should print 2.
questions.explain: has tells "cached as undefined" apart from "not cached", so Bola's second call is a hit too.

questions.q: Use Map.groupBy to group the orders by status, then print one line per status with the number of orders and the total in naira, in order of first appearance.
questions.explain: Each group is an array of the original objects. Iterating the map gives [key, group] pairs in the order keys first appeared.

questions.q: Write latestById(events) that returns an array with one event per orderId: the last one for each id, in order of each id's first appearance.
questions.explain: Later pairs overwrite earlier values, but an existing key keeps its position, which gives exactly "last value, first position".

questions.q: Write setFee(fees, sku, city, kobo) and getFee(fees, sku, city) using nested maps (a map from SKU to a map from city to fee). getFee returns undefined for unknown products or cities.
questions.explain: Optional chaining (?.) returns undefined when the product has no inner map, instead of throwing.

questions.q: Print the customers who have an open cart but no entry in lastOrder, using a set method with the map as its argument.
questions.explain: A map is set-like through its keys, so difference works directly without building a set of ids.

questions.q: Convert the stock Map and the tags Set to JSON so no data is lost, then parse the JSON back into a Map and a Set and print 2 true.
questions.explain: JSON only knows objects and arrays. Object.fromEntries and spread convert on the way out; Object.entries and the constructors rebuild on the way in.
